items.name: Caral & Norte Chico
items.description: The Norte Chico (Caral–Supe) civilisation on Peru's north-central coast built monumental platform mounds and sunken plazas from roughly 3000 BCE, making Caral one of the oldest known cities in the Americas. Its people fished the Pacific, farmed cotton and squash by irrigation, and apparently built on this scale without pottery or large-scale warfare. Caral was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009.

items.name: Chavín Culture
items.description: Centred on the highland temple of Chavín de Huántar, the Chavín culture spread a shared religious art style — jaguars, serpents, and fanged deities like the carved Lanzón — across much of Peru. Chavín de Huántar's stone galleries and channels were designed for ritual effect, and its iconography influenced later Andean cultures for centuries.

items.name: Nazca & Moche
items.description: Two great regional cultures flourished in parallel. On the south coast the Nazca etched vast geoglyphs — the Nazca Lines — into the desert and made polychrome pottery. On the north coast the Moche built adobe pyramids such as the Huacas del Sol y de la Luna and produced some of the most realistic portrait ceramics of the ancient world; the unlooted tomb of the Lord of Sipán, excavated in 1987, revealed their metalwork.

items.name: Wari & Chimú
items.description: The Wari state, based near modern Ayacucho, built an early highland empire with administrative centres and roads that the Inca later echoed. After Wari's collapse, the coastal Kingdom of Chimor (Chimú) ruled the north coast from Chan Chan, the largest adobe city in the Americas, until the Inca conquered it around 1470.

items.name: Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu)
items.description: From Cusco, Pachacuti and his successors built Tawantinsuyu, the largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas, stretching from modern Ecuador to central Chile. It ran on the mit'a labour system, a road network of tens of thousands of kilometres, and khipu knotted-cord records. A succession war between Atahualpa and Huáscar left it exposed when Francisco Pizarro captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532; the Neo-Inca state held out in Vilcabamba until 1572.

items.name: Viceroyalty of Peru
items.description: Spain governed most of South America from Lima, founded in 1535, through the Viceroyalty of Peru. Silver from Potosí, mined largely through forced indigenous labour, flowed into global trade. Epidemics and the colonial labour system devastated Andean populations. Late in the period, Bourbon reforms sharpened grievances, and Túpac Amaru II's rebellion of 1780–1781 was one of the largest indigenous uprisings in colonial history.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Rebellion of Túpac Amaru II

items.name: Republic of Peru
items.description: José de San Martín proclaimed independence in Lima on 28 July 1821, and the Battle of Ayacucho (1824) ended Spanish rule. A guano export boom was followed by defeat in the War of the Pacific (1879–1884), which cost Peru its southern nitrate provinces to Chile. The 20th century swung between oligarchic, populist, and military governments. From 1980 the Shining Path insurgency and state repression killed tens of thousands; Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission estimated about 69,000 deaths. Alberto Fujimori's government (1990–2000) defeated the insurgency but ended in scandal, and later democratic politics have been marked by repeated presidential crises.
